chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from more than one (narrator), from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
'There is nothing among the things that God, Mighty and Majestic, has made permissible that is more hateful to Him than divorce, and indeed God hates the frequent divorcer, al-dhawwaq (the taster).'

key_terms.الذَّوَّاق: Al-dhawwaq: Literally 'the taster' or 'the sampler'; a man who repeatedly marries and divorces women, treating marriage as a casual pleasure rather than a serious commitment.
key_terms.الطَّلَاق: Talaq: Islamic divorce, particularly the husband's unilateral pronouncement of divorce. Though legally valid, it is considered among the most disliked permitted acts.
key_terms.الْمِطْلَاق: Al-mitlaq: An intensive form indicating habitual or repeated divorcing; one who divorces excessively or casually.
key_terms.عَزَّ وَجَلَّ: Azza wa Jalla: 'Mighty and Majestic', a common epithet for God emphasizing His transcendent power and greatness.

ai.seo_question: What does Islam say about divorce — is it permissible but disliked?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) teaches that while divorce is legally permissible in Islam, it is among the most detestable permitted acts in God's sight. The term 'al-dhawwaq' (the taster) refers to a man who repeatedly marries and divorces women as if sampling them, which the hadith characterizes as especially hateful to God. This teaching reflects the Islamic principle that legal permissibility does not imply divine approval, and that the stability of the family institution is deeply valued in Islamic jurisprudence.
word_analysis: the taster (one who repeatedly samples wives)
